meta.title: Who really said "And now we welcome the new year, full of things that have never been"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Rilke wrote it, but not that way. The famous New Year line paraphrases his 1 January 1907 letter to Clara from Capri. Here is the genuine wording, sourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'And now we welcome the new year, full of things that have never been'?
meta.ogDescription: The New Year line credited to Rilke is a paraphrase of his 1 January 1907 letter to Clara Rilke from Capri. The real sentence, with translator and page.

answer.label: Paraphrased from Rainer Maria Rilke
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Rilke’s and the letter is real — but the greeting-card wording is not his. Writing to his wife Clara from the Villa Discopoli on Capri on 1 January 1907, Rilke ended the letter, “And now let us believe in a long year that is given to us, new, untouched, full of things that have never been…” (1945 Greene & Norton translation ↗). The popular line replaces “let us believe in a long year that is given to us” with “we welcome the new year” — a rewrite, not a translation.

source.heading: The letter it really comes from

docMeta.dd: Jane Bannard Greene & M. D. Herter Norton (W. W. Norton, 1945), p. 253

source.excerpt: And now let us believe in a long year that is given to us, new, untouched, full of things that have never been…
trail: The genuine sentence closes a letter headed “To Clara Rilke — Villa Discopoli, Capri (Italy), January 1, 1907.” The full text is readable in the scanned 1945 Greene and Norton translation ↗, whose translators’ note says the letters were taken from the Insel-Verlag collection edited by Rilke’s daughter and son-in-law, Ruth Sieber-Rilke and Carl Sieber.

WIST Quotations ↗, a sourced quotation database, files the passage under that exact letter date and records that it is commonly shortened to “And now we welcome the new year. Full of things that have never been.”
Wikiquote’s Rilke page ↗ carries no entry for the New Year line at all — not in its sourced material and not among its flagged attributions. Quote Investigator has not published on it either.
A magazine essay, “The Poetry Resolution” ↗, begins with a holiday card printed with the short line, traces it to the Capri letter, and notes that the card’s wording differs from the letter’s.
source.excerptNote: The published sentence runs on past this point — work that has never been done, tasks, claims and demands — and closes the letter. Wording is the 1945 Greene and Norton translation, which is still under copyright, so only the opening clause is reproduced here.

author.name: Rainer Maria Rilke
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote the sentence
author.heading: Rilke on a Capri rooftop, 1 January 1907
author.metaLine: 1875–1926 · Austrian poet · Letter to Clara Rilke, Capri, 1 January 1907
author.bio: Rainer Maria Rilke was born in Prague in 1875 and died in Switzerland in 1926, and is one of the most widely translated poets in the German language — best known for the Duino Elegies, the Sonnets to Orpheus, and Letters to a Young Poet. He married the sculptor Clara Westhoff in 1901; the correspondence between them runs for decades and is a substantial part of his published work. The New Year sentence comes not from a poem but from one of those letters, written from Capri while the two were living apart.

misattribution.heading: What went wrong on the way to the greeting card
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote — there is a real letter, on a real date, in a real book. What has gone missing is Rilke’s actual sentence. The circulating version keeps six words of the published translation and replaces the rest.

items.who: Greeting cards, quote-image sites and social posts
items.why: The published English reads “And now let us believe in a long year that is given to us, new, untouched, full of things that have never been…” The popular line swaps the opening clause for “we welcome the new year,” which is a rewrite rather than a variant rendering — the German turns on believing in a year that has been given, not on welcoming one (1945 translation, in full ↗).
Both list the short form under Rilke’s name with no letter, no date, no book and no translator; Goodreads adds that its quotes are community-submitted and unverified (AZQuotes entry ↗).

items.who: Anthologies and social graphics that present it as a poem
items.why: It is prose from private correspondence, not verse. The passage has been broken into lines and typeset as a New Year poem in several arrangements, which is part of why the wording drifts (on the recast versions ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is Rilke’s, and it is datable to the day — 1 January 1907, in a letter to Clara Rilke from Capri — but the fourteen-word version on the card is a condensation nobody has traced to a published translation (letter and paraphrase, side by side ↗).

context.heading: What he was actually looking at
lead: Rilke spent that New Year’s Eve alone. Clara was in Germany; he was staying at the Villa Discopoli on Capri. He went out after eleven expecting a midnight Mass, and the letter he wrote the next morning describes what he found instead: lanes striped black and white by wall-shadow and the first moon after the full, olive leaves cut out of night sky, a knot of Capri youths on the little piazza under the clock tower, a tambourine rattling out of a red-curtained coffee-house — and a church shut, “as if it had been closed for decades.”

Only after all that does the famous sentence arrive. He had gone back to his little house and climbed up on its roof, wanting to see a good end in what had passed and find a good beginning in himself. The line is not a toast to a crowd; it is one husband asking his absent wife to believe in the year with him.
context.detailsSummary: The German, and why the short version travels better
detailsBody: In German the key phrase is voll nie gewesener Dinge — “full of things that have never been” — inside a sentence that begins with believing in a long year that has been given to us (German text and letter context ↗). The half that survived into greeting cards is the half that needs no grammar around it.

The prose passage has also been recast and typeset as a poem in various forms, which is part of why the wording drifts so freely: once a sentence from a letter is broken into lines, nobody expects it to match a page in a book.
context.pull: Rilke did not welcome the new year. He asked Clara to believe in it.

sourcesVerified.claim: The volume contains a letter headed "To Clara Rilke — Villa Discopoli, Capri (Italy), January 1, 1907" ending "And now let us believe in a long year that is given to us, new, untouched, full of things that have never been, full of work that has never been done..."; the front matter reads "Copyright, 1945, by W. W. Norton & Company, Inc."; the translators' note says the letters come from the Insel-Verlag collection edited by Ruth Sieber-Rilke and Carl Sieber.

Internet Archive metadata for the scanned book gives the title "Letters Of Rainer Maria Rilke 1892 1910", publisher W. W. Norton and Company Inc., year 1945, with Jane Bannard Greene and M. D. Herter Norton credited.

WIST files the full passage under "Letter (1907-01-01) to Clara Rilke", citing Letters of Rainer Maria Rilke p. 253, and notes the quotation is commonly shortened to "And now we welcome the new year. Full of things that have never been."

Wikiquote's Rainer Maria Rilke page contains no entry for "And now we welcome the new year" or "full of things that have never been", and no reference to the 1 January 1907 letter to Clara Rilke, in any section.

Goodreads displays "And now we welcome the new year, full of things that have never been" attributed to Rainer Maria Rilke with no book, letter or date cited, and states that quotes are added by the community and not verified.
AZQuotes displays "And now we welcome the new year, full of things that have never been" credited to Rainer Maria Rilke with no source documentation of any kind.

The Pacific Standard essay describes a holiday card reading "And now we welcome the new year, full of things that have never been", traces it to the letter Rilke sent Clara in January 1907 while writing from Capri, and remarks that the letter's text is a slightly different translation than the card's.
W. W. Norton lists Letters of Rainer Maria Rilke, 1892-1910, translated by Jane B. Greene and M. D. Herter Norton, as one of its titles.
Rainer Maria Rilke was born 4 December 1875 in Prague and died 29 December 1926 in Switzerland; he was an Austrian poet writing chiefly in German and married Clara Westhoff in 1901.

The post gives the German original of the passage, beginning "wollen wir glauben an ein langes Jahr, das uns gegeben ist, neu, unberührt, voll nie gewesener Dinge...", identifies it as from Rilke's 1 January 1907 letter to Clara from Capri, and notes the prose passage has been recast into poems in various typesettings.
